front: Define the law of one price for a market \((X, p)\).
back: Any two portfolios with the same payoff have the same cost: \(X\theta = X\theta' \Rightarrow p^\top\theta = p^\top\theta'\).

front: State the law of one price as a condition on the kernel of \(X\).
back: \(p^\top\theta = 0\) for every \(\theta \in \ker X\), i.e. \(p \perp \ker X\) (Proposition 2.2).

front: Define a state-price vector.
back: A vector \(\psi \in \R^S\) with \(X^\top\psi = p\): \(p_n = \sum_s \psi_s X_{sn}\). \(\psi_s\) is the value of one unit paid in state \(s\) only.

front: State the three equivalent faces of the law of one price (Theorem 2.4).
back: (i) the law of one price; (ii) a unique linear pricing functional \(q\) on the payoff space \(M\) with \(q(X\theta) = p^\top\theta\); (iii) a state-price vector with \(X^\top\psi = p\).

front: How many state-price vectors does a market satisfying the law of one price have?
back: An affine subspace \(\psi_0 + \ker X^\top\) of dimension \(S - \operatorname{rank} X\); unique iff \(M = \R^S\) (Proposition 2.6).

front: What price does the law of one price assign to a new payoff \(z\)?
back: If \(z \in M\), exactly \(q(z) = p^\top\theta_z\) for any replicating \(\theta_z\); if \(z \notin M\), any price (Proposition 3.1).

front: With a riskless payoff traded, what do the entries of any state-price vector sum to?
back: The riskless payoff's price, \(\sum_s \psi_s = q(\mathbf 1) = 1/R_f\) (Example 5.1).

front: Lab 2: how close are the one-month DKK and EUR spot payoffs, 1999-02 to 2026-09?
back: A regression of DKK on EUR has \(R^2 = 0.99891\) and a residual s.d. of 8.65 bp a month (against 261.9 bp for the payoff); the ten-currency second-moment matrix has condition number \(2.776 \times 10^7\).
basis: Lab 2 (single sample: H.10 month-end spot rates, retrieved 2026-10-19)

front: In Shleifer and Vishny's model, what can happen to arbitrage by specialized investors using other people's money?
back: Arbitrageurs who are fully invested when a mispricing deepens lose funds and are forced to cut their positions, so arbitrage can become least effective when the mispricing is largest (Proposition 3, p. 45).

front: Derive the forward price of a currency from the law of one price.
back: Dollar bond, foreign bond and forward replicate each other state by state: \(F = \mathcal S_0(1 + r)/(1 + r^\ast)\), whatever the distribution of \(\mathcal S_1\) (Example 3.2).

front: Misconception: “the law of one price says every asset has a price.”
back: It says payoffs, not assets, have prices. With no redundant asset it holds for every price vector and restricts nothing.

front: Misconception: “state prices are positive.”
back: Under the law of one price alone they can be negative (Lab 1 at \(t = 0.7\)); positivity needs no arbitrage (Lesson 2).

front: Misconception: “payoffs with correlation 0.999 are redundant.”
back: Redundancy is an exact linear relation in every state; a nearly redundant payoff is outside the span of the other and is not priced by the law of one price.

front: Define an arbitrage in a one-period market.
back: A portfolio with \(X\theta \ge 0\), \(p^\top\theta \le 0\) and a nonzero cash-flow vector \((-p^\top\theta, X\theta)\).

front: Does no arbitrage imply the law of one price? Conversely?
back: Yes (Proposition 1.2). Not conversely: one asset paying 1 at price \(-1\) satisfies the law of one price and is an arbitrage.

front: State the separation lemma used in Lesson 2.
back: A subspace \(L\) missing a nonempty compact convex \(K\) admits \(w \perp L\) with \(w^\top k \ge \|w\|^2 > 0\) on \(K\); \(w = Qk^\ast\) at the point of \(K\) nearest \(L\) (Lemma 2.1).

front: State the fundamental theorem of asset pricing for one period and finitely many states.
back: No arbitrage iff some \(\psi \gg 0\) satisfies \(X^\top\psi = p\) (Theorem 3.1).

front: In the proof of the finite FTAP, how are state prices read off the separating vector \(w\)?
back: \(w \perp L\) gives \(X^\top w_{1:S} = w_0 p\); with \(w \gg 0\), set \(\psi = w_{1:S}/w_0\).

front: Why does the FTAP proof separate \(L\) from the simplex rather than from the orthant?
back: The simplex is compact, so the distance to \(L\) is attained and \(w \ne 0\); the orthant minus the origin has distance zero to \(L\) (Problem P3).

front: Bond \((1,1,1)\) at 0.96, stock \((1.4, 1.1, 0.6)\). For which stock prices is there no arbitrage?
back: The open interval \((0.576, 1.344)\): \(0.96\) times the payoff range (Example 3.4).

front: When can a new payoff \(z\) be added at price \(c\) without arbitrage?
back: Iff \(c = \psi^\top z\) for some strictly positive state-price vector of the original market (Proposition 4.1).

front: Misconception: “a zero state price is fine, since it is not negative.”
back: The FTAP needs strictly positive state prices; at a zero state price there is an arbitrage that pays in that state (Example 3.4 at \(c = 0.576\)).

front: Misconception: “a high expected return relative to risk is an arbitrage.”
back: Arbitrage never loses in any state and does not involve probabilities; a strategy that can lose is a bet.

front: Misconception: “no arbitrage makes state prices unique.”
back: It gives some strictly positive vector; uniqueness needs \(\operatorname{rank} X = S\).

front: Write the arbitrage detection program.
back: \(\sup_\theta \mathbf 1^\top X\theta - p^\top\theta\) s.t. \(0 \le X\theta \le \mathbf 1\), \(0 \le -p^\top\theta \le 1\).

front: What does the detection program's value tell you?
back: It is feasible with \(0 \le V \le S + 1\), and an arbitrage exists iff \(V > 0\) (Proposition 2.2).

front: What certificates settle whether a market has an arbitrage?
back: Either a portfolio with nonnegative cash flows of positive sum, or a strictly positive \(\psi\) with \(X^\top\psi = p\); exactly one exists, and each is checked by matrix multiplication (Theorem 3.1).

front: Define the state-price margin and its role.
back: \(t^\ast = \sup\{t \le 1 : X^\top\psi = p, \psi \ge t\mathbf 1\}\); no arbitrage iff \(t^\ast > 0\) (Proposition 3.2).

front: State super-replication duality.
back: If \(M\) contains a strictly positive payoff and there is no arbitrage, \(\min\{p^\top\theta : X\theta \ge z\} = \max\{\psi^\top z : \psi \ge 0, X^\top\psi = p\}\), both attained; similarly for sub-replication (Theorem 4.1).

front: What is the set of arbitrage-free prices of a payoff \(z \notin M\)?
back: The open interval between its sub- and super-replication bounds (Corollary 4.2).

front: Bond and stock of Example 4.3; call paying \((0.4, 0.1, 0)\). Arbitrage bounds?
How do arbitrage bounds change when a spanned payoff \(y\) is added to \(z\)?
back: Both shift by \(q(y)\): general put–call parity (Problem P3).

front: Misconception: “a payoff can be quoted at its upper arbitrage bound.”
back: Unspanned payoffs' arbitrage-free prices form an open interval; at the bound, selling the payoff against its super-replicating portfolio is an arbitrage.

front: Misconception: “detection value 0 means every price is fair.”
back: It means some strictly positive state-price vector prices everything; with fewer assets than states many do, and prices can be shaded without arbitrage (Lab 1).

front: Define a stochastic discount factor.
back: A random variable \(m\) with \(p = \E[m x]\) for every traded payoff.

front: How do SDFs relate to state prices?
back: \(m = \psi/\pi\) entrywise is a bijection from state-price vectors to SDFs that preserves signs (Proposition 2.1).

front: When does an SDF exist? A strictly positive one?
back: An SDF iff the law of one price holds; a strictly positive SDF iff there is no arbitrage (Theorem 2.2).

front: State the Riesz representation theorem used in Lesson 4.
back: On a finite-dimensional real inner-product space every linear functional is \(f(v) = \langle v^\ast, v\rangle\) for exactly one \(v^\ast\) (Theorem 3.1).

front: State the existence and uniqueness of the SDF in the payoff space.
back: Under the law of one price exactly one SDF lies in \(M\), \(x^\ast\); with independent payoffs \(x^\ast = x^\top \E[xx^\top]^{-1}p\) (Theorem 3.2).

front: When is the SDF unique?
back: Iff the market is complete, \(M = \R^S\); then it is \(x^\ast\) (Corollary 3.3).

front: How is every SDF related to \(x^\ast\)?
back: \(m = x^\ast + \varepsilon\) with \(\E[\varepsilon x] = 0\); \(x^\ast\) is the projection of every SDF on \(M\) and \(\E[m^2] = \E[x^{\ast2}] + \E[\varepsilon^2]\) (Theorem 4.1).

front: Can \(x^\ast\) be negative in a market with no arbitrage?
back: Yes: one payoff \((3, 1, -1)\) priced by \(m = (1.2, 0.9, 0.8)\) with \(\pi = (0.25, 0.5, 0.25)\) gives \(x^\ast = (1.15, 0.383, -0.383)\) (Example 5.1). It is positive in a complete market.

front: What is the price of the payoff \(x^\ast\)?
back: \(\E[x^{\ast2}] = p^\top\E[xx^\top]^{-1}p\) (Problem P1).

front: Why is \(x^\ast\)'s weight vector a regression coefficient?
back: The no-intercept regression of any SDF on \(x\) has normal equations \(\E[xx^\top]\beta = \E[xm] = p\) (Problem P3).

front: Misconception: “the SDF is unique.”
back: Only in a complete market; otherwise the SDFs are \(x^\ast + M^\perp\), and prices identify only \(x^\ast\).

front: Misconception: “an SDF needs a model of preferences.”
back: Its existence follows from the law of one price, and \(x^\ast\) is computed from prices and payoffs alone.

front: Misconception: “the SDF's mean is one.”
back: With a riskless payoff it is \(1/R_f\).

front: Define \(R^\ast\) and state its extremal property.
back: \(R^\ast = x^\ast/\E[x^{\ast2}]\), the return on \(x^\ast\); it has the smallest second moment of all returns in \(M\), \(1/\E[x^{\ast2}]\) (Theorem 1.3).

front: State the minimum-variance SDF with mean \(v\).
back: \(m_v = v + (x - \mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(p - v\mu)\), with variance \((p - v\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(p - v\mu)\), for invertible \(\Sigma\) (Theorem 2.1).

front: With a riskless payoff, which SDF has the least variance?
back: \(x^\ast\), since every SDF has mean \(1/R_f\) (Proposition 2.2).

front: State the variance bound.
back: \(\sigma(m)/|\E[m]| \ge |\E[R^e]|/\sigma(R^e)\) for every SDF and every excess return; with a riskless payoff, \(\sigma(m)/\E[m] \ge\) any Sharpe ratio (Theorem 2.4).

front: Which SDF attains the variance bound, and what does it equal?
back: \(x^\ast\) (with a riskless payoff): the maximum Sharpe ratio in \(M\) equals \(\sigma(x^\ast)/\E[x^\ast]\) (Corollary 2.5).

front: Which duality do Lesson 5's Theorems 2.1 and 2.4 prove, and whose idea is it?
back: The SDF's least volatility at each mean, \(\sigma_{\min}(v)\), is dual to the largest Sharpe ratio of the returns, without imposing \(m \ge 0\); the duality is Hansen and Jagannathan's, whose frontier also imposes positivity.

front: Describe the mean-variance frontier in SDF terms.
back: The minimum-variance returns are \(R^\ast + wR^{e\ast}\), with \(R^{e\ast}\) the projection of 1 on the excess returns; with a riskless payoff, \(R^{e\ast} = (R_f - R^\ast)/R_f\) (Theorem 3.2, Problem P3).

front: With a riskless payoff, how does \(\E[R^\ast]\) compare with \(R_f\)?
back: \(\E[R^\ast] < R_f\) whenever \(\Var(x^\ast) > 0\): \(R^\ast\) is on the lower branch of the frontier (Problem P3).

front: State the expected-return–SDF identity and its beta form.
back: \(\E[R] - R_f = -R_f\Cov(m, R)\) for every SDF; \(= \beta_{R,R^\ast}(\E[R^\ast] - R_f)\) (Theorem 4.1).

front: Misconception: “\(R^\ast\) is the tangency portfolio.”
back: It is the minimum-second-moment return, with mean below \(R_f\); it prices by beta but no Sharpe-maximizer holds it long.

front: Misconception: “an SDF above the variance bound is a good model.”
back: The bound is necessary, not sufficient; an SDF above it can still misprice assets.

front: Misconception: “without a riskless asset there is no variance bound.”
back: The bound is a curve \(\sigma_{\min}(v)\) in the SDF's mean.

front: Define an equivalent martingale measure in one period.
back: A probability \(\mathbb Q\) positive on every possible state with \(p_k = \E^{\mathbb Q}[x_k]/R_f\) for every asset.

front: How are EMMs and SDFs related?
back: \(\mathbb Q(\{s\}) = R_f\pi_s m_s\): a bijection from strictly positive SDFs to EMMs, with \(d\mathbb Q/d\Prob = R_f m\); under no arbitrage the EMM is unique iff the market is complete (Theorem 1.2).

front: State the fundamental theorem on a finite tree.
back: Finite \(\Omega\), finitely many dates, predictable strategies: no arbitrage iff an EMM exists under which discounted prices are martingales (Theorem 3.2).

front: How is the EMM constructed in the proof of the multiperiod theorem?
back: Apply the one-period theorem to each node's market of discounted increments and the constant; the node state prices are transition probabilities, multiplied along paths.

front: How is an attained payoff priced on a tree?
back: \(\E^{\mathbb Q}[H/B_n]\), the same under every EMM (Corollary 3.3).

front: Doubling on a fair coin with horizon \(n\): win probability, mean gain, expected deepest loss?
Why is doubling excluded by the general theorems?
back: They allow only admissible strategies, whose wealth is bounded below; doubling needs unbounded credit.

front: State the Delbaen–Schachermayer theorem for locally bounded processes.
back: A locally bounded semimartingale admits an equivalent local martingale measure iff it satisfies no free lunch with vanishing risk.

front: Misconception: “risk-neutral pricing assumes risk-neutral investors.”
back: \(\mathbb Q\) is a rescaled positive SDF and can reflect any risk aversion; it absorbs risk premia into probabilities.

front: Misconception: “any probability that prices the assets is an EMM.”
back: It must be equivalent to \(\Prob\), positive on every possible state; boundary measures with a zero are not EMMs.

front: Misconception: “in continuous time, no arbitrage iff an EMM exists.”
back: The general theorem needs no free lunch with vanishing risk, admissible strategies, and gives a local martingale measure for locally bounded prices.

front: Why are the sample \(x^\ast\)'s in-sample pricing errors uninformative?
back: \(\E_T[\hat x^\ast x] = \hat S\hat S^{-1}p = p\) for any data with invertible \(\hat S\) (Proposition 2.1).

front: When are the sample \(x^\ast\) weights consistent?
back: When \(\hat S \to S\) in probability, by continuity of \(A \mapsto A^{-1}p\) on invertible matrices (Proposition 3.1).

front: Why is \(A \mapsto p^\top A^{-1}p\) convex?
back: It equals \(\sup_c(2c^\top p - c^\top Ac)\), a supremum of functions affine in \(A\) (Lemma 3.2).

front: Which way is the sample \(x^\ast\)'s second moment biased?
back: Upward: \(\E[p^\top\hat S^{-1}p] \ge p^\top S^{-1}p\) by Jensen, when \(\E[\hat S] = S\) (Theorem 3.3).

front: What is ridge shrinkage of SDF weights, as a projection?
back: \((\hat S + \lambda I)^{-1}p\) minimizes \(\E_T[(m - x^\top c)^2] + \lambda\|c\|^2\) for any sample SDF; in-sample errors are \(-\lambda\hat b_\lambda\) (Proposition 4.2).

front: Lab 2: out-of-sample pricing of nine currency payoffs, trained 1999-02 to 2012-11, tested 2012-12 to 2026-09?
back: Test rms error 270.0 bp for the sample \(x^\ast\), 80.2 bp for validated ridge, 20.1 bp for the constant \(m = 1\).
basis: Lab 2 (single sample: H.10 month-end spot rates, retrieved 2026-10-19)

front: Misconception: “zero in-sample errors show the estimated SDF fits.”
back: They hold by construction for any data; only out-of-sample errors are evidence.

front: Misconception: “choose the shrinkage that minimizes test errors.”
back: A parameter chosen on the test sample is fitted to it; choose it inside the training sample.

front: Misconception: “consistency means the sample SDF's volatility is a good estimate.”
back: In every finite sample its second moment is biased upward (Theorem 3.3).

front: State Proposition 2.3 of Lesson 5.
back: When \(\Sigma\) is invertible, \(x^\ast\) is the minimum-variance SDF at its own mean: \(x^\ast = m_{v^\ast}\) with \(v^\ast = \E[x^\ast]\).

front: What does no arbitrage imply for the pricing functional on payoffs?
back: \(q\) is strictly positive on \(M\): a nonnegative nonzero payoff has a positive price, and \(R_f = 1/\sum_s\psi_s > 0\) (Corollary 3.3).

front: State the law of one price as a range condition.
back: It holds iff \(p \in \operatorname{range}(X^\top)\) (Corollary 2.5).

front: On a tree, define a trading strategy, its discounted gain and an arbitrage.
back: A predictable \(\phi_t \in \R^K\), financed by the bond; \(G_n(\phi) = \sum_t \phi_t^\top(\tilde S_t - \tilde S_{t-1})\); an arbitrage has \(G_n \ge 0\) everywhere and \(> 0\) somewhere (Definition 2.1).

front: Define out-of-sample pricing errors.
back: Estimate \(\hat b\) on the training sample only; \(e = \E_{\mathcal V}[x\,x^\top\hat b] - p\) on the later test sample, with root mean square \(\sqrt{\tfrac1N\sum_n e_n^2}\) (Definition 4.1).

front: Misconception: “if the market has state prices, they are unique.”
back: Only if \(\operatorname{rank} X = S\); otherwise they form an affine subspace of dimension \(S - \operatorname{rank} X\) (Proposition 2.6).

front: Misconception: “the arbitrage bounds are the range of a payoff's discounted expected value.”
back: They are the extremes of \(\psi^\top z\) over nonnegative state prices (Theorem 4.1) and do not involve the probabilities.

front: Misconception: “the box in the detection program limits the size of the arbitrage.”
back: Arbitrages form a cone; the box picks one representative per ray and only decides whether one exists.

front: Misconception: “a single-factor beta model that prices all returns proves the factor is a risk factor.”
back: Any frontier return prices every return exactly by construction (Theorem 4.1); it is a statement about the assets used, not about economic risk.

front: Misconception: “a strategy that wins with probability one is an arbitrage.”
back: Doubling needs unbounded credit; on every finite horizon its mean gain is zero, with a loss of \(2^n - 1\) with probability \(2^{-n}\) (Proposition 5.1).

front: Misconception: “ridge shrinkage is ad hoc, with no pricing interpretation.”
back: It is the penalized projection of any SDF on the payoffs, with in-sample pricing errors \(-\lambda\hat b_\lambda\) (Proposition 4.2).
